newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government shuns senator's vote.
newsitem.headline: Australian government shuns senator's vote.

text.p: A key independent Australian senator under fire over corruption allegations faced mounting pressure on Wednesday to quit politics, with the government saying it would no longer accept his vote.

Prime Minister John Howard, who has seen his public support slip over his handling of the scandal, said he still considered senator Mal Colston innocent pending the outcome of police investigations, but said the government would no longer accept the Labor defector's support in the upper house.

Howard's year-old conservative government does not have a Senate majority and has relied on support from Colston and another independent to pass key reforms, including budget cuts, through the Senate.
"In all of the circumstances if Senator Colston remains a member of the Senate we will not in future accept his vote," Howard said in a radio interview.

"And the way that we will not accept his vote is to arrange that if he does decide to support the government on an issue we will arrange for one of our number to drop out of the division (vote) so that his vote is not in effect counted."

But the government's action is more symbolic than practical, since it can still pass legislation if Colston does not vote with the Labor opposition -- effectively maintaining the current situation. The balance of power in the Senate will now be held by another independent, Tasmanian Brian Harradine.

Howard has joined Labor and the Australian Democrats in demanding Colston quit the influential post of Senate deputy president. But he stopped short on Tuesday of backing their demands that Colston quit the Senate altogether.
Colston, who is in a Brisbane hospital suffering from a lung infection, denies any illegal activity and has refused to announce any decision on his poltical future until he recovers.

The government, Labor and the Democrats have all said they would dump Colston from the deputy presidency if he did not step aside voluntarily by the time the Senate resumes on May 6. But the Senate does not have the power to vote to expel a senator.
Labor rejected as a political stunt Howard's call to match the government's decision to reject Colston's vote.

"Mal Colston's vote is a tainted vote and so is his absence, because it's just about as good for the government to have Colston's vote nullified as it is to have his vote," opposition leader Kim Beazley said in a radio interview.
"What we want is for John Howard to do what he should have done months ago ... tell this bloke to get out of parliament and allow the Queensland people to be properly represented."

If Colston is forced out of parliament -- whether by a fraud conviction or political pressure -- the constitution requires him to be replaced by a Labor member because he was originally elected as a Labor senator.

This would alter the balance of power because Labor, the Democrats and a thid minor leftist party, the Greens, could then muster a combined 38 votes in the 76-seat chamber, enough to block government legislation.
